text: Chrome plating has been highly favored for its advantages (e.g., high hardness, excellent corrosion resistance, and wear resistance), whereas the environmental pollution and health hazards arising from hexavalent chromium in the plating solution have aroused rising attention. 1,2 Electroplated Ni− Co−P alloy coatings have been considered a promising alternative to chrome plating for their prominent thermal stability, corrosion resistance, and wear resistance, as reported in existing research. 3−6 However, several problems (e.g., severe hydrogen evolution at the cathode and unstable plating solution) during the electroplating process of Ni−W−B alloy coatings can trigger cracked coatings, lack of metallic luster, and inadequate decorative properties. 7,8 Accordingly, the electroplating process of the Ni−W−B alloy should be investigated in depth.

text: Additives take on critical significance in electroplating, even though they are employed in small quantities. They exert notable efects on the performance exhibited by the plating solutions and coatings. Surfactants are capable of reducing the surface tension of the plating solution such that the plating solution can spread more smoothly on the substrate surface. Moreover, surfactants facilitate the release of hydrogen gas adsorbed on the cathode surface such that the occurrence of pinholes and pitting on the coating surface can be reduced and a smoother surface can be generated. Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), i.e., a commonly used surfactant, can efectively hinder the formation of pinholes and pitting in coatings. 9 However, excessive addition can lead to rough coatings. Song et al. 10 investigated the efects exerted by three diferent surfactants on the performance of electroplated ${ \mathrm { N i - P } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { A l } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ composite coatings. As indicated by the results, the addition of SDS leads to optimal stability in the plating solution, resulting in uniform coatings with improved hardness and corrosion resistance compared with coatings with cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS), or triethanolamine (TEOA). The addition of brighteners notably enhances the glossiness of the coatings, resulting in a mirrorlike surface. Moreover, it can enhance hardness, corrosion resistance, and other properties. Zhu et al. 11 investigated the efects of thiourea, 1,4-butyne diol, and sodium saccharin on the electroplated tin−nickel−copper alloy coatings. To be specific, they determined the optimal additive formulation using response surface methodology (RSM), such that gun black tin−nickel−copper alloy coatings with excellent corrosion resistance, high hardness, and brightness were prepared. The use of appropriate additives can refine the grain structure of ${ \mathrm { N i } } { - } \mathrm { C o }$ alloy coatings, resulting in higher hardness. Furthermore, the addition of an appropriate amount of 1,4-butyne diol can produce uniform and bright Ni−W alloy coatings. 13,14 However, the addition of 1,4-butyne diol can decrease the current eficiency. Adding a suitable amount of auxiliary brighteners to the plating solution has been considered to be a common method to facilitate the distribution of the plating solution and achieve diverse coating properties. Matsui et al. 13 introduced sodium allyl sulfonate (ALS), sodium saccharin, and other additives to Ni−W alloy and identified improvements in properties $\left( \mathrm { e . g . } \right.$ , tensile elongation). The performance of the plating solution and coatings can be significantly enhanced by the addition of appropriate additives. 15−18

text: The efects of additives on _ Ni-Co-P coatings in electroplating have rarely been investigated. In this study, the preliminary screening of surfactants and brighteners was conducted through single-factor experiments based on the basic formulation of the electroplated Ni−Co−P alloy. RSM was employed to design experiments and investigate the efects of additives ( e.g., SDS, thiourea, and ALS) on the hardness and glossiness of the coatings. Stable plating solutions and coatings with excellent performance were obtained through compre hensive analysis and optimization. This study aimed at providing more insights into the efects of process conditions and plating solution composition on the coating performance. It can lay a solid basis for in-depth research on N i - C o - P and its composite coatings while providing a useful reference for the industrial production of electroplated Ni−Co−P compo site coatings.

The parameters for impedance testing comprised a frequency range of 0.01 to 10,000 Hz and a scanning rate of 10 Hz/s.

text: 4.1. Single-Factor Experiments. 4.1.1. Efect of Surfactant on Coating Hardness. The addition of the surfactant SDS to the plating solution was investigated to determine its efect on coating performance. The results, shown in Figure 1, indicate that as the SDS concentration increased, the porosity of the coating decreased and the hardness increased. When the SDS concentration reached 0.1 g / L, the coating exhibited the lowest porosity of 0.23 pores/ cm ^ 2 and the maximum hardness of 4 0 8.4 HV _ 0.5. However, further increasing the SDS concentration led to an increase in coating porosity and a decrease in hardness. The appropriate addition of SDS facilitated the forward shift of the nucleation potential and reduced cathodic polarization during deposition, 19 which can contribute to coating formation. Moreover, it lowered the surface tension of the plating solution, thus facilitating the easy release of hydrogen gas generated during the hydrogen evolution reaction on the cathode surface. Thus, the formation of pinholes and pitting was reduced, resulting in a lower coating porosity and a denser coating structure, leading to an increase in hardness. However, excessive surfactant concentration can cause the aggregation of surfactant molecules, forming micelles, thus afecting the deposition process and resulting in decreased coating hardness and increased porosity.

text: To better understand the efects of diferent additives on coating hardness, 3D response surface plots depicting the interaction efects of the additives on coating hardness were constructed, as shown in Figure 5. Under the ALS concentration of 0.2 g / L, the interaction efects of diferent concentrations of SDS and thiourea on coating hardness are shown in Figure 5a. For various concentrations of thiourea, the efect of the SDS concentration on coating hardness is consistent, and the fluctuation in coating hardness is minimal. As the SDS concentration was increased from 0.08 to 0.1 2g/ L, the coating hardness initially increased slightly and then decreased. For diferent concentrations of SDS, the efect of thiourea on coating hardness follows a similar pattern but with larger fluctuations in coating hardness. When the thiourea concentration was increased from 0.1 to 0.18 g/L, the coating hardness first increased significantly and then decreased. The addition of an appropriate amount of SDS reduces the surface tension of the plating solution, allowing it to spread better on the cathode, resulting in a tighter bond between the coating and substrate and reducing the formation of coating defects. The addition of an appropriate amount of thiourea forms an adsorption layer on the cathode surface and forms complexes with metal cations in the solution, making it more dificult for the metal ions to discharge and increasing the overpotential of the deposition reaction, thereby promoting nucleation and refining the coating’s crystalline structure. The combined action of appropriate concentrations of SDS and thiourea reduces the surface tension of the plating solution, promotes nucleation, and enhances the coating hardness. However, excessive amounts of SDS and thiourea can lead to dificulties in the discharge of metal ions and increased hydrogen evolution, resulting in a decrease in the coating hardness.

text: To better illustrate the efects of the additives on coating glossiness, 3D response surface plots depicting the interaction efects of the additives on coating glossiness were constructed, as shown in Figure 6. Under a constant concentration of ALS, the interaction efects of diferent concentrations of SDS and thiourea on the coating glossiness are shown in Figure 6a. When SDS concentration was at a low level, coating glossiness significantly increased with the rise in thiourea concentration. However, when SDS concentration was at a high level, coating glossiness increased with the rise in thiourea concentration but with a smaller magnitude. When thiourea was at a low level, increasing SDS concentration led to a slight increase in coating glossiness. However, when thiourea was at a high level, increasing SDS concentration progressively decreased coating glossiness. The addition of thiourea forms a tightly adsorbed layer on the cathode surface, increasing the dificulty of metal ion discharge, enhancing the overpotential of the reaction, and promoting nucleation. Meanwhile, thiourea facilitates hydrogen evolution. When SDS concentration was at a low level, the reduction in surface tension of the plating solution improved the detachment of hydrogen gas from the cathode surface, resulting in finer coating grains and reduced defects such as pinholes, leading to a significant increase in coating glossiness. However, when SDS concentration was at a high level, the normal deposition of metal ions was somewhat afected, resulting in a smaller increase in coating glossiness. When thiourea concentration was at a low level, the hydrogen evolution phenomenon did not achieve significance, and increasing SDS concentration led to a slight increase in coating glossiness. However, when thiourea concentration was at a high level, increasing SDS concentration favored hydrogen evolution, which afects the deposition of metal ions, resulting in a gradual decrease in coating glossiness.

text: 4.3. Efect of Additives on Coating Surface and Performance. The surface morphology of the coatings obtained with the additive-containing plating bath was identified and analyzed by using SEM and compared with the morphology of coatings obtained without additives. Figure 9 presents the results. As depicted in Figure 9, the coating surface obtained without additives had numerous grain-like protrusions, and even pinholes could be identified at 8000 times magnification. In contrast, the coating surface obtained with the additive-containing plating bath had fewer grain-like protrusions and no identified defects ( e.g., pinholes). The coating surface was smooth, flat, and dense, suggesting that the addition of additives can significantly enhance the smoothness and compactness of the coating, contributing to the enhance ment of the coating performance.

text: EDS analysis was conducted on the coatings obtained from the additive-containing plating bath and compared with the coatings obtained without additives. The results are presented in Figure 10. After adding additives to the plating bath, the elemental composition in the coating was Ni 71.01 at %, Co 20.65 at %, and P 8.34 at %. The Ni content in the coating increased, while the Co content decreased slightly compared with the coating obtained from the plating bath without additives. The P content did not show a significant change. The possible reason for the above result is the anomalous codeposition behavior of nickel and cobalt. The standard electrode potential of Ni ^ 2 + was −0.250 V, while that of Co ^ 2 + was −0.277 V. Co ^ 2 + shows a more negative potential and tends to deposit preferentially. The addition of additives can increase the overpotential of the reaction, making the discharge of metal ions more dificult while afecting the preferential deposition of Co ^ 2 +, leading to a slight decrease in the cobalt content in the coating. Figure 11 presents EDS mapping of the _ Ni-Co-P coating obtained from the additive-containing plating bath, demonstrating the uniform distribution of Ni, Co, and P elements throughout the coating.

text: Through the Box−Behnken experiment for additive formula tion, the optimal additive combination was determined to be an SDS concentration of 0.10 g/L, thiourea concentration of 0.15 g/L, and ALS concentration of 0.22 g / L. The coatings obtained under these optimized additive conditions exhibited a hardness of 4 7 5.4 HV _ 0.5, which was 9 0.3 4 HV _ 0.5 higher than that of the coating without additives. The glossiness of the coating was 463.4GU, which increased by 101.2GU compared with the coating without additives. The corrosion resistance of the coatings was also improved. The addition of additives improved the surface morphology of the coatings, making them smoother and more compact. The addition of the optimized additive combination significantly improved the coating performance, resulting in coatings with a metallic luster similar to stainless steel, which meets industrial requirements.
